The elements of the grounds are extracted roughly in this order:

* Caffeine
* Flavor/Aromatic oils
* Bittering agents

The first brew is going to get the caffeine and flavor oils and some of the bittering agents. Any subsequent brews are just going to extract more bittering agents, leaving you with flavorless, bitter coffee with very little caffeine content.

You can see this by making a simple coffee method. Set a pot of water to boil. Dump in some coffee grounds, and taste the coffee after 5 seconds, 30 seconds, 1 minute, 5 minutes, 10 minutes. Your first taste will taste like dirty water. Later tastes will taste like what you think of as coffee - oily mouthfeel with some bitterness. The longer you let the coffee sit there boiling, the more it'll just taste of bitterness.

Games from your list I'm familiar with:

* **A city-building game.** Another rule simple game. On your turn, buy a tile, place a tile, and then adjust your income/reputation/population/assets as noted. Obtain your income, increase/decrease your population, and your turn is over. The challenge is figuring out how to balance your income and reputation to win.

* **A tile-placement game.** Figuring out how the tiles work together is the hardest part. But relatively simple. Roll two dice, use the dice to obtain tiles, place tiles or sell goods. The rule book is somewhat of a mess - it gets more detailed than it needs to be.

* **A palace-building game.** Because of the choices, this one is a touch more difficult, but still learnable in 10 minutes. On your turn, draw money, buy a tile, place a tile from reserve, or swap two tiles' locations. The first two actions are easy to understand, but figuring out how to effectively use the reserve pile and tile swapping can be somewhat maddening.

At some point, to make a game a game, there needs to be some abstraction.

To take an example from another game... I played a lot of a popular MMORPG until recently. For years, when you gained levels, you'd have to periodically return to your Class Trainer to purchase training in your new abilities. From an immersion/realism standpoint, this was great. It wouldn't make sense that just because I leveled up, I would have all these new techniques - no, it made sense that I'd have to return to a trainer to obtain knowledge. But in action, it just bogged the game down. Or the stealth class used to need to purchase materials to mix poisons to apply to their weapons. Great immersion. But in effect, it meant that if I wanted a certain number of instant poisons, deadly poisons, and crippling poisons for the night's raid, I had to do some math to figure out how much of each material to buy and then hit the craft button and wait to mix them into poisons - not fun.
In a survival situation, it's a sure fire way to get hypothermia to consume snow.

Then it comes down to "will this mechanic add to the experience/difficulty, or just adding a thing you have to do?"

Take a recent game update as an example. It adds immersion, for sure - it's not realistic or immersive to spend months on end sleeping for 10 hours, drinking water, sleeping 10 more hours, occasionally eating. Obviously, that's broken, both for gameplay and immersion - there's nothing fun about being incentivized to spend every moment from a certain point onward in a single location drinking and eating, leaving at most once a week.

But many "immersive" changes do nothing more than add mechanics that require you to "do" something. A ridiculous example would be waking/running. Right now I press forward on my joystick and move. That's not nearly as immersive if I had to alternate pressing buttons to move my left foot, right foot, etc. But a change like that would just make the game annoying.

That said, I'll echo most of the other posters here that actually playing is the best thing to learn. My usual practice with a new game is ...

* Read the rulebook

* Read the rulebook again while unboxing -- identify all the bits and pieces, location of places on the board where bits will go, etc.

* Play a mock game against myself. Can't emphasize how helpful this is. You really figure out then why a phase is "play, THEN draw" rather than "Draw, then play". Or how board movement works, or where a draw and discard pile is. You learn the pacing of the game, so that when you're teaching you can note that the first 3 turns are a prologue to the game, or that it's around round 10 that everything becomes a storm.
